title: Query execution: iterators, joins and vectors
goal: By the end, you can explain how a database runs a plan as a chain of steps that pull one row at a time, predict the work a nested loop, hash or merge join does and find it in EXPLAIN ANALYZE, and say why passing rows in batches, or compiling each query, beats one row at a time, and when.
opening:
Picture asking a friend in a second-hand bookshop for five novels priced under 5. They don't list every book in the shop first. They walk along the shelves, check each price, and come back the moment they have five.

Now ask for the five cheapest novels in the shop. They can't come back until they've seen every price, because the cheapest one might be on the last shelf.

It's easy to picture a database doing the first job the slow way: read the whole table, then keep what was asked for. That's how many of us would write it, one step after another, each finished before the next begins. A database runs a query more like the friend.

In Indexes for text, time and vectors, we built indexes that find rows. In this lesson, we'll follow the rows once they're found: how the steps of a plan hand them on, how a join pairs two tables, and why handing them over in batches is far faster. Before we start, make a guess, and keep it in mind.

warmup.q: A table of 100,000 payments has no index on the amount, and about 1 payment in 10 is over 900.00. You ask for any 5 of those: `SELECT id FROM payments WHERE amount_cents > 90000 LIMIT 5`. (Amounts are stored in cents, and `LIMIT 5` means "stop at 5 rows".) Roughly how many rows does the database read?
options: All 100,000: it has to check every row before it can pick 5
About 50 or 60: it stops reading once it has 5 rows
Exactly 5
About 10,000: every matching row, of which it then keeps 5
warmup.why: PostgreSQL's executor pulls rows. The LIMIT step asks the filter for a row, the filter asks the scan until a row passes, and after the fifth row the LIMIT stops asking. With 1 row in 10 matching, the scan reads about 50 rows; the first Try it shows 62. Reading all 100,000 is what happens when every step builds its whole result before passing it on. Exactly 5 would need an index that finds only matching rows.

sections.h: A plan is a tree of steps that pull rows one at a time
sections.body:
The last few lessons were about where rows live and how indexes find them. Something has to run the query that uses them. A query is a question written in SQL, the language databases understand, and the part of the database that runs it is the executor. Take the warm-up's query on PostgreSQL, the free database program this course uses: `SELECT id, amount_cents FROM payments WHERE amount_cents > 90000 LIMIT 5`. It asks a table of 100,000 card payments, one row per payment, for any 5 rows above 900.00. (A small company's program records each card payment at a shop, with amounts in cents.)

Before anything runs, the planner, the part that decides how to answer, turns the query into a **plan**: a tree of small operators that each do one job. A scan reads the table, a filter keeps the rows that pass the WHERE condition, and a limit stops after 5 rows. EXPLAIN, PostgreSQL's command for showing a plan, prints that tree with the root at the top and the scan at the bottom. How the planner chooses is the next lesson's subject. This one is about how rows move through the tree.

Version 1 runs each operator to the end and hands its whole result to the next. The scan reads all 100,000 payments into a list, the filter builds a second list of the 10,000 that pass, and the limit keeps 5 and throws the rest away. It works. But it holds whole in-between results in memory, which a table of 200 million rows won't fit, and it reads 100,000 rows to answer a question about 5. That's the friend who carries the whole shop to the counter.

Version 2 turns the flow around. Every operator has the same three methods: `open()` to get ready, `next()` to return one row (or null when there are no more), and `close()` to clean up. An operator gets its input by calling `next()` on its child, the operator below it. To produce a row, the limit calls the filter's `next()`. The filter calls the scan's `next()` until a row passes, and that row travels back up. After the fifth row, the limit returns null without calling its child again, so the scan never reads another row. Nothing is collected in a list: each operator holds one row at a time.

This is the **iterator model**, also called the Volcano model after Goetz Graefe's research system from the early 1990s. PostgreSQL's executor works this way, and its documentation calls it "a demand-pull pipeline". In Kotlin terms it's a `Sequence` rather than a `List`: `payments.asSequence().filter { it.amount > 90_000 }.take(5)` stops after five matches. In the bookshop, each `next()` is you saying "one more, please", the filter is your friend checking the price, and the scan is the walk along the shelves. The picture breaks in one place: your friend keeps walking on their own, while an operator moves only when its parent asks.

The stepper shows the calls going down and the rows coming up. In the Try it, the Seq Scan under the Limit returns 5 rows and throws away 57, so it read 62 of the 100,000 rows. Without the LIMIT, it reads them all and throws away 90,001.

Some operators can't pass rows on one at a time. A sort can't return its first row before it has seen every input row, because the last row read might sort first: that's the friend asked for the five cheapest books. So on its first `next()`, a sort pulls its whole input, sorts it, and then hands rows out one per call. Grouping rows with a hash table, the lookup table of the third section, works the same way. These are called blocking operators, or pipeline breakers, and they're where memory limits come in: `work_mem` sets how much memory each may use before it spills to temporary files on disk.

A scan, a filter and a limit each have one child. Next comes an operator with two: the join.

frames.say: The client closes the plan, and `close()` travels down so each operator can let go of what it holds: pages it pinned in memory, working memory, temporary files. Count the work: 4 rows read, 2 returned, 6 `next()` calls on the scan side. A plan that built full lists would have read all 6, or all 100,000.

```text

-------------------------------------------------------

   ->  Seq Scan on payments (actual rows=5.00 loops=1)

----------------------------------------------------

With the LIMIT, the scan returned 5 rows and threw away 57: it read 62 rows and stopped, because the Limit stopped asking. Without it, the scan read all 100,000. The filter is printed as a line of the Seq Scan node, because PostgreSQL checks simple WHERE conditions inside the scan instead of in a separate operator; it's the same pull. `max_parallel_workers_per_gather = 0` turns off parallel query (splitting a big scan between several processes) for your session, so each plan runs in one process and the trees stay small.

sections.h: Joining two tables, version 1: a nested loop compares every pair
sections.body:
Now a join: each payment with its shop's name. `payments` has 100,000 rows and `merchants` has 1,000 (the code calls a shop a merchant). The condition is `m.id = p.merchant_id`: a payment belongs to the shop whose `id` equals the payment's `merchant_id`. Those two columns are the join keys. A join is an operator with two children, called the outer and the inner, and its `next()` must return the next matching pair.

Version 1 is the **nested loop join**, the two for-loops anyone would write. For each outer row, scan the whole inner input and return every pair whose keys are equal. In iterator terms, the join closes and reopens its inner child for every outer row. The cost is outer rows times inner rows: 1,000 x 100,000 = 100 million comparisons to produce 100,000 pairs. In the Try it, PostgreSQL was forced into this plan. It put the merchants outside, scanned all of `payments` once per merchant (`loops=1000`), reported `Rows Removed by Join Filter: 99900000` and took about 14 seconds.

You may be thinking that nobody would run that on purpose. PostgreSQL agrees, which is why the Try it has to switch the other choices off by hand.

The cost multiplies, so the fix is to make the inner side cheap. Say the inner table has an index on the join key: a B+tree (the lesson B+trees), a tree of pages that keeps keys sorted, so finding one key takes three or four page reads. Then the join does one index lookup per outer row instead of a full scan. Most of those page reads come from the buffer pool, PostgreSQL's cache of pages in memory, so they cost little. That's the **index nested loop join**, and for a small outer side it's the best plan there is. In the Try it, joining 10 payments to their merchants does 10 index lookups and touches 10 merchant rows.

A nested loop is also the only join that works for any condition, such as `p.amount_cents > m.daily_limit_cents` (payments above their shop's daily limit), because it compares every pair.

Reading the numbers needs one rule. EXPLAIN reports a node that ran several times as an average per run. `actual rows=1.00 loops=10` means the inner index scan ran 10 times and returned 1 row each time on average, 10 rows in total. Multiply rows by loops to get the total. PostgreSQL 18 prints rows with two decimals because they're averages.

A nested loop is cheap when one side is tiny or indexed. When both sides are big and nothing is indexed, we need another idea. Next: a lookup table.

sections.h: Version 2, the hash join: build a lookup table, then read each side once
sections.body:
For an equality join on two big inputs, there's a better idea: build a lookup table first. The **hash join** reads the smaller input completely into a hash table keyed on the join column. A hash table turns each key into a slot number, so finding a key takes one step, like a Kotlin `HashMap`. That's the build phase, and it happens before the first row comes out. Then the join pulls rows from the other input one at a time and looks up each one's key: the probe phase.

Each input is read once, so the work grows with outer plus inner rows: 101,000 row reads instead of 100 million comparisons. In the Try it, the hash join takes tens of milliseconds where the nested loop took 14 seconds. The build side is a pipeline breaker; the probe side streams.

Two limits come with it. It works only for equality: a hash table answers "which rows have key 17", never "which rows have a key below 17". And the table needs memory. PostgreSQL allows a hash table `work_mem` times `hash_mem_multiplier`, 4 MB times 2 by default. If the build side doesn't fit, the join splits both inputs into batches by hash value, writes the batches to temporary files and joins them one pair at a time. EXPLAIN then shows `Batches: 4` instead of 1, and the join still finishes, with extra disk work.

The third classic join is the **merge join**. If both inputs arrive sorted on the join key, walk them side by side, the way you'd merge two sorted piles of cards. Always take from the side with the smaller key. Each side is read once, and nothing extra is held in memory. It shines when the order comes free, for example from a B+tree index scan, or when the result must be sorted anyway. When the order isn't free, the merge join has to sort first. In the Try it, it sorts all 100,000 payments, spilling 2.5 MB to a temporary file, and it's slower than the hash join.

The figure puts the three side by side. The planner chooses among them from its estimates of how many rows each side will have, and the next lesson shows how. The rough rule: index nested loop for a small outer side with an index on the inner, hash join for big unsorted equality joins, and merge join when both inputs already come sorted.

All three joins still pass one row per `next()` call. On a query that reads millions of rows, that habit itself becomes the cost. Next, we'll measure it.

sections.h: Version 3 of running a plan: pass a thousand values per call
sections.body:
The iterator model costs something on every row. For each row, each operator calls its child's `next()` without knowing what kind of operator the child is. With many kinds of operator behind one call, the CPU (the chip that runs the instructions) can't predict well where the call goes. The WHERE condition is worked out by walking a tree of expressions, one node per part of the condition. For `amount_cents > 9000`, the comparison itself takes well under a nanosecond, a billionth of a second. The machinery around it takes many times that. On a query that touches 10 rows through an index, nobody notices. On a report query that reads 100 million rows, it's most of the time.

The MonetDB/X100 researchers at CWI in Amsterdam measured exactly this in 2005 (Boncz, Zukowski and Nes). They ran query 1 of TPC-H, a standard test made of report queries: a scan of 6 million order lines that computes sums and averages. On MySQL 4.1, a popular free database program, it took 26.6 seconds of CPU time. A profile, a measurement of where the time goes, showed that the actual additions and multiplications took under 10% of it. One addition cost about 49 CPU cycles (ticks of the CPU's clock). Every function call computed a single value, so the CPU could never overlap the work of two rows. A hand-written C program did the whole query in 0.22 seconds.

Vectorized execution changes the unit of work. `next()` returns a batch of values stored by column, all the amounts together, so a filter runs one tight loop over a plain array of amounts. There are no calls inside the loop and no expression tree. The CPU can overlap the work of many rows, and the compiler can turn the loop into SIMD instructions, which compare several values in one step. The cost of a call is paid once per batch instead of once per row. In the bookshop, it's your friend bringing a crate of books per trip instead of one book.

X100 ran query 1 in 0.50 seconds: over 50 times faster than MySQL, and about twice as slow as the hand-written program. Its batches held 1,024 values, and the size matters. At 1 value per batch, the MySQL overhead came back. Around 1,000 was fastest. Above about 8,000, the batches no longer fit in the CPU cache, the small, fast memory on the chip, and it slowed down again. DuckDB, a free database program built for reports, runs every query this way, with vectors of 2,048 values (`STANDARD_VECTOR_SIZE`). Column stores and compression, lesson 11 of this track, covers the column storage it pairs with.

In the Try it, the lab's demo runs the same filter and sum over 10 million payments three ways. In the run shown, the row-at-a-time pipeline took 13.9 ns per row, batches of 1,024 took 1.9 ns, and a hand-written loop 0.33 ns. That last line is the next section's subject.

Why does PostgreSQL keep the iterator model? Its typical query finds a few rows through an index, where the cost per row is noise, and the model keeps every operator small and easy to combine. DuckDB is built for the other end, scans over millions of rows. Your lab builds both: the iterator operators, then a vectorized filter that pulls batches of 1,024.

steps: Read `VectorDemo.kt`: the same `sum(amount) WHERE amount > 9000` as a Volcano pipeline, as batches of 1,024, and as one plain loop.
From the `labs` folder, run the demo (no Docker needed). Predict the ratio between the Volcano time and the batch time.

rows: 10,000,000   matching sum: 9,490,500,000
plan             cpu ms     ns/row
volcano           139.3      13.93
vectorized         18.8       1.88
plain loop          3.3       0.33
```

Here the Volcano pipeline needed about 7 times as long per row as the batch pipeline, and the plain loop was about 6 times faster again. Your numbers depend on your CPU, your JDK (the Java toolkit that runs the demo) and what else the machine is doing. The demo prints the best of 5 runs to soften that, and the order stays the same. The batch version spends its time in two loops with no calls inside. The Volcano version makes a `next()` call per row per operator and works out the WHERE condition by walking an expression tree. sections.h: Version 4: compile one loop per query, and pay to compile it
sections.body:
Batches are one way to stop paying for the machinery on every row. The other is to stop interpreting, which means working through a description of the query step by step. Instead, generate code for this one query and compile it, the way a compiler turns Kotlin into machine instructions. Thomas Neumann's HyPer, a research database, did this in 2011. Its compiler cuts the plan at the pipeline breakers from the first section. It turns each pipeline (a scan, its filters, and the hash table or total it feeds) into one loop. That loop keeps the current row in CPU registers, the few storage slots inside the chip, from start to end. No `next()` calls are left. It's the demo's plain loop, written by the database.

HyPer generated code for LLVM, a toolkit that turns a portable form of code into machine code, and that took milliseconds. Its first version generated C++, another programming language, and waited seconds for the C++ compiler. TPC-CH is a test that mixes everyday work with reports. On its query 1, a sum by group over the order lines of 12 warehouses, HyPer took 35 ms on one CPU core with everything in memory. VectorWise, the product X100 became, took 98 ms, MonetDB (the research database X100 grew out of) 72 ms, and a traditional disk-based database 4,221 ms. Compiling cost 16 to 41 ms per query with LLVM, and 1.5 to 2.6 seconds with C++.

So which design wins? In 2018, Kersten, Leis, Kemper, Neumann, Pavlo and Boncz built both into one test system, with the same hash tables and the same use of several cores. They found the two surprisingly close on report queries. Compiled code runs fewer instructions, so it wins when a query computes a lot on data already in the CPU cache. Vectorized code keeps more memory reads going at once, so it wins when a query spends its time waiting on large hash tables for joins and grouping. SIMD helped less than expected, because most of the time goes to waiting for memory.

The cost that comparison sets aside is compile time. 16 ms is nothing next to a 10-second report, and a lot next to a 2 ms lookup. PostgreSQL's JIT shows it. JIT, just-in-time compilation, means compiling code while the program runs. Since version 11, PostgreSQL can compile a query's expressions and its row decoding (turning a page's bytes into column values) with LLVM once the query's estimated cost passes `jit_above_cost` (100,000). In the Try it, a 100,000-row sum took 7.8 ms without JIT, and 76 ms with full JIT optimization, 69 ms of it compiling. PostgreSQL 19, a release candidate in November 2026, turns JIT off by default.

Most of today's new engines are vectorized libraries that others build databases from, such as Meta's Velox and Apache DataFusion; the Deeper notes say where they run. And every design in this lesson runs whatever plan it's given. None of them chooses the plan, and a fast executor running a bad plan is still slow.

With inlining and optimization, LLVM spent 69 ms of the 76. On a scan of 100 million rows, the same compile cost would be small next to the time saved, which is why PostgreSQL only compiles queries whose estimated cost is high. Your times will differ; the order won't. The plan's `cost=` numbers are shown here only because the `JIT:` section is printed with them.

worked.title: Trace a hash join on five rows

steps.say: The build side is three shops, and the probe side is four payments, one of them with no shop (a null merchant). The join is `HashJoin(build = merchants, probe = payments, buildKey = 0, probeKey = 1)`.
steps.code:
merchants (id, name):   (1, Acme)  (2, Bolt)  (3, Cord)
payments (id, merchant): (p1, 2)  (p2, null)  (p3, 1)  (p4, 2)

steps.say: `open()` runs the build phase: it pulls every row from the build side into a hash table from key to rows, then opens the probe side. Nothing has been read from `payments` yet.
Each `next()` first hands out any waiting matches for the current probe row. When there are none, it pulls the next probe row and looks its key up once.
Call `next()` four times. p2's null key skips the lookup. None of the calls reads the build side again.
steps.code:
next() -> pulls p1, key 2 -> (2, Bolt, p1, 2)
next() -> pulls p2, key null, no lookup; pulls p3, key 1 -> (1, Acme, p3, 1)
next() -> pulls p4, key 2 -> (2, Bolt, p4, 2)
next() -> probe returns null -> null

steps.say: Count the work. The hash join read 3 build rows and 4 probe rows, and did 3 lookups. A nested loop over the same inputs would have examined 4 x 3 = 12 pairs. With 100,000 payments and 1,000 merchants, that's 101,000 reads against 100 million comparisons.
steps.code:
hash join:    build 3 rows + probe 4 rows, 3 lookups
nested loop:  4 outer rows x 3 inner rows = 12 comparisons

lab.title: Build a Volcano executor with joins and a vectorized filter
steps: Read the top of `Operators.kt`: the `Operator` interface, `Scan`, and `Unary`, which opens and closes its child for you. Then read the `Counting` wrapper at the top of `ExecutorTest.kt`: it's how the tests see what each operator pulled.
Run the tests once from the `labs` folder (no Docker needed). All 11 fail.
Write `next()` for `Filter`, `Project` and `Limit`. The pipeline and limit tests pass.
Write `open()` and `next()` for `NestedLoopJoin`, then for `HashJoin`. The join tests compare your hash join with your nested loop join on random data with repeated and null keys.
Write `BatchFilter.nextBatch()` in `Vectors.kt`, and run the tests until all 11 pass. Then run the demo from the fourth Try it again and read its code next to yours.
hints: `Limit.next()` must check its count before it calls `child.next()`. If it calls first and checks after, it pulls one row too many, and the limit test counts the scan's rows.

In `NestedLoopJoin`, keep the current outer row in `outer`. When the inner side returns null, take the next outer row; if there is none, return null; otherwise `right.close()` and `right.open()` to scan it again, and loop.
In `HashJoin`, a waiting list of matches for the current probe row (an `Iterator<Row>`) is the whole trick: one probe row can match several build rows, and `next()` returns them one call at a time.
In `BatchFilter`, collect the passing positions first, then copy those positions of every column. Skip a batch where nothing passed: the tests check that you never return an empty batch.

drill.title: Write a nested loop join from memory
drill.prompt: Close the lab. Write `open()` and `next()` of a `NestedLoopJoin(left, right, leftKey, rightKey)` over the `Operator` interface (`open`, `next(): Row?`, `close`). It returns `leftRow + rightRow` for every pair with equal keys that aren't null, and scans the right side again for every left row. Then say how many times the right side is opened for 100 left rows.

recap: A plan is a tree of operators with `open`, `next` and `close`. Each `next()` pulls one row from below, so LIMIT stops the scan early and nothing is collected in lists. Sorts and hash-table builds are pipeline breakers: they read all their input first.
A nested loop join costs outer x inner comparisons. With an index on the inner side, it becomes one lookup per outer row, the best plan for a small outer side.

A hash join builds a table from the smaller side and probes it once per row of the other: about outer + inner work, equality only, and batches on disk when the table outgrows `work_mem`. A merge join walks two inputs sorted on the key.

One row at a time spends most of a report query on overhead: MySQL spent over 90% of TPC-H query 1 outside the arithmetic. Vectorized engines (X100, DuckDB, Velox, DataFusion) pass batches of about a thousand values and run tight loops over arrays.

Compiled engines (HyPer) generate one loop per pipeline and keep rows in CPU registers. The two designs end up close: compiled wins on computation, vectorized on joins and grouping that wait on memory.

The limit: compiling costs milliseconds per query, which can be more than the query itself (PostgreSQL's JIT made a 100,000-row sum slower, and PostgreSQL 19 turns JIT off by default), and no executor can rescue a badly chosen plan.
closing:
We started with a friend in a bookshop who came back with five cheap novels before seeing every book. The executor works the same way: LIMIT 5 read 62 rows of 100,000. A hash join read each table once where a nested loop compared 100 million pairs, and batches of 1,024 cut the cost per row about seven times.

If you have psql open, run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE)` on a query with a join and find the join's node. Is it a Nested Loop, a Hash Join or a Merge Join, and what are its children's `loops`?

Next, we'll see how the planner chooses among all these plans without running any. How does it guess how many rows each step will return?

quiz.q: EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows `Index Scan using merchants_pkey on merchants m (actual rows=1.00 loops=250)` under a Nested Loop. How many shop rows did this node return in total?
options: It can't be known from this line
quiz.why: For a node that runs several times, EXPLAIN shows rows as an average per run. The inner index scan ran 250 times, once per outer row, and returned 1 row each time on average: 250 rows in total. Reading `rows=1.00` as the total is the classic mistake, and it hides that the node ran 250 times.

quiz.q: Join 2 million payments with a table of 50 card companies on `network_id`. Neither table has an index on the join columns, and nothing is sorted. Which join does the least work?
options: Nested loop with the card companies outside: 50 scans of 2 million rows
Nested loop with the payments outside: 2 million scans of 50 rows
Hash join building a table of the 50 card companies and probing it once per payment
Merge join after sorting both tables
quiz.why: The hash join reads each table once: 50 rows to build a tiny table, then 2 million probes, about 2 million units of work. Either nested loop examines 100 million pairs. A merge join would first sort 2 million rows, which costs more than hashing them, since nothing arrives sorted.

quiz.q: A program's lookups take about 3 ms each. Someone sets `jit_above_cost = 0` for its database user, so that "every query gets compiled". What happens?
options: Every lookup gets about 3 times faster, because compiled code runs in registers
Nothing, because PostgreSQL only compiles queries that scan more than 100,000 rows
Only the first run of each query pays to compile; later runs reuse the machine code
Most lookups get slower, because each query now pays milliseconds of LLVM compilation that its few rows can never earn back
quiz.why: PostgreSQL compiles at the start of every run of the query and keeps nothing for the next one. In the Try it, compiling a 100,000-row sum turned 8 ms into 25 ms, and into 76 ms with optimization. A lookup that touches a few rows has nothing to win back. `jit_above_cost` exists so that only expensive queries pay, and its 100,000 is an estimated cost, not a row count.

quiz.q: From B+trees: an index nested loop join looks up the shops of 10,000 payments in a B+tree of height 3 (three levels of pages) on `merchants.id`. Roughly how many index page reads does that take, and why is it cheaper than it sounds?
options: About 30,000, three per lookup from root to leaf, but the root and the level below it stay in the buffer pool, so most are memory hits
10,000, one per lookup
3, because the tree is read once and reused
About 10 million, because each lookup scans the leaf level
quiz.why: Each lookup goes down from the root through one inner level to a leaf: three page reads. The root and the inner pages are touched by every lookup, so they stay in the buffer pool, the page cache from The buffer pool, and only leaf pages may need a disk read. Scanning the whole leaf level is exactly what a B+tree lets you avoid.

quiz.q: On one CPU core, why does a vectorized filter over 10 million amounts run several times faster than a Volcano filter over the same data?
options: It reads less data from disk
It pays the call overhead once per batch and spends its time in a tight loop over an array that the CPU can pipeline and the compiler can vectorize
It uses an index to skip rows
It runs the batches on several threads
quiz.why: Both read the same values, on one thread, with no index. The Volcano filter makes calls and walks an expression for every row. The vectorized one makes one call per 1,024 rows and runs a loop with no calls inside, which modern CPUs and JIT compilers run very fast. The demo measured 13.9 ns per row against 1.9.

flashcards.front: What are the three methods of an operator in the iterator (Volcano) model?
flashcards.back: `open()` to get ready, `next()` to return one row or null at the end, `close()` to clean up. Parents call `next()` on their children.
An operator that must read all its input before returning its first row, such as a sort or the build side of a hash join.

flashcards.front: How much work does a nested loop join do?
flashcards.back: Outer rows x inner rows comparisons. With an index on the inner key, one index lookup per outer row instead.

flashcards.front: What are the two phases of a hash join?
flashcards.back: Build: read the smaller input into a hash table on the join key. Probe: read the other input once and look up each row's key.

flashcards.front: What does a compiled query engine like HyPer generate?
flashcards.back: One loop per pipeline (a scan and its filters, up to the next hash table or total) that keeps the current row in CPU registers, with no `next()` calls. HyPer compiled it with LLVM in tens of milliseconds.

flashcards.front: How do you read `rows=1.00 loops=250` in EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
flashcards.back: The node ran 250 times and returned 1 row per run on average: 250 rows in total. Multiply rows by loops.

flashcards.front: What is vectorized execution, and what batch size works?
flashcards.back: Operators pass batches of values stored by column and handle each batch in a tight loop. X100 found about 1,000 best: 1 brings back the cost per row, and above about 8,000 a batch no longer fits in the CPU cache. DuckDB uses 2,048.

terms.plain: Generating and compiling code for each query, so a whole pipeline runs as one loop, as HyPer does.
Every operator has open, next and close, and pulls one row at a time from its children.
An operator that takes in all its input before it produces any output, such as a sort or a hash-table build.
For each outer row, scan the inner input and return the matching pairs.
A nested loop whose inner side is an index lookup on the join key, one per outer row.
Build a hash table from one input, then probe it with each row of the other. Equality joins only.
Walk two inputs sorted on the join key side by side, as when merging two sorted lists.
Operators pass batches of about a thousand values, stored by column, instead of one row per call.

explain_back.prompt: A teammate ran the same join twice, once with `enable_hashjoin = off`, and saw 50 ms against 9 seconds. Explain what the executor did differently in the two runs, using the iterator model and the row counts in the plans.
explain_back.answer: Both plans are trees of operators that pull rows with `next()`. In the fast run, the hash join first pulled all 1,000 merchants from its build child into a hash table. Then it pulled the 100,000 payments one at a time and looked each one's merchant id up in the table: about 101,000 rows read and 100,000 lookups. In the slow run, the planner could only use a nested loop. For each of the 1,000 merchants, it closed and reopened the payments scan and compared every payment, so the inner scan ran 1,000 times (`loops=1000`) and 100 million pairs were examined, of which 99.9 million were thrown away (`Rows Removed by Join Filter`). The join produced the same 100,000 rows both times; the nested loop did a thousand times more work to find them. A nested loop is only fast when the outer side is small and the inner side is an index lookup.

deeper.body:
**Grouping and sorting.** GROUP BY runs either as a hash aggregate (a hash table from each group's key to its running totals, the `HashAggregate` in the Try its) or as a sort followed by a group aggregate that streams through runs of equal keys. When the input doesn't fit in `work_mem`, a sort writes sorted runs to temporary files and merges them, the external merge sort you see as `Sort Method: external merge`. Hash aggregation spills batches the way the hash join does.

**Parallel query.** With parallel workers turned on, PostgreSQL runs copies of the lower part of a plan in several processes, and a `Gather` node pulls their rows together; a hash join can even build one shared hash table. The Try its turned this off to keep the trees small. HyPer and DuckDB split the work into small morsels of rows that idle threads pick up, which keeps every core busy without planning the split in advance. Kersten and colleagues found that both compiled and vectorized engines scale well this way.

**Push instead of pull.** A compiled pipeline runs from the bottom up: the scan's loop pushes each row into the filter and on into the hash table, with no parent asking for it. Many vectorized engines push batches too. The result is the same set of rows; what changes is who holds the loop.

**Memoize.** Since PostgreSQL 14, a nested loop's inner side can sit behind a `Memoize` node, a small cache from join key to result. When many outer rows share a key, as 100,000 payments share 1,000 merchants, the inner lookup runs once per distinct key and every repeat is a cache hit. That's why the second Try it turned it off.

**Engines as libraries.** Velox is Meta's vectorized engine, written in C++ and used in more than a dozen of its systems. Prestissimo swaps the Java workers of Presto, a query engine, for it, and Gluten runs Spark SQL on it (Spark is a program that runs one job across many machines). Apache DataFusion is an engine written in Rust on the Arrow column format. InfluxDB 3 runs on it, and Comet uses it to run Spark plans natively. The Batch processing and analytics track meets them again where Spark runs.

**A tempting fix that isn't one.** When one join is slow and EXPLAIN shows a nested loop, it's tempting to set `enable_nestloop = off` for the whole server. That one query gets faster, and hundreds of others that relied on index nested loops switch to hash joins that scan whole tables. Usually the real cause is a bad row estimate: the planner expected 10 outer rows and got 100,000, which the next lesson covers. Fix the estimate (`ANALYZE`, extended statistics, a better index), or as a last resort set the flag with `SET LOCAL` inside that one transaction.
